claims.text: Post-deposition nitriding can convert the outer part of an elemental Cr coating into a continuous, thin CrN layer.
The CrN layer will prevent premature coating failure by inhibiting elevated-temperature Cr-Zr interdiffusion.
The nitrided coating will retain protective oxidation and corrosion resistance under both subcritical water and high-temperature steam.
The initial material is an elemental Cr coating on zirconium-alloy cladding without an engineered diffusion barrier.
A controlled nitrogen-plasma or equivalent nitriding process can form an ultrathin, interfacially continuous CrN layer on the coating.
Approximately 300°C represents normal subcritical-water operation, while temperatures up to approximately 1000°C represent accident-relevant steam exposure.
A CrN layer at or near the Cr/Zr interface acts as a physical barrier to atomic diffusion.
CrN exhibits much lower atomic diffusivity than the unmodified coating material relevant to Cr-Zr interdiffusion.
The CrN barrier slows mutual diffusion between Cr and Zr at elevated temperature.
Slowing Cr-Zr interdiffusion inhibits the formation of interdiffused, less-protective phases.
The CrN-containing coating will still permit formation of a protective oxide such as Cr2O3 under normal operating conditions.
Dense oxide formation can provide corrosion resistance for accident-tolerant-fuel cladding coatings.
Relative to untreated Cr, the nitrided coating will have a reduced Cr-Zr interdiffusion-zone depth.
Relative to untreated Cr, the nitrided coating will form thinner and more stable oxide scales.
Relative to untreated Cr, the nitrided coating will have improved high-temperature stability.
Nitriding will not compromise the coating's corrosion protection in subcritical water.
An unmodified elemental Cr coating on zirconium-alloy cladding undergoes elevated Cr-Zr interdiffusion in high-temperature steam, leading to premature coating failure.
Relevant exposure durations are hours for accident-temperature steam and thousands of hours for normal-operation subcritical water.
The reduction in interdiffusion kinetics and the optimal CrN thickness and uniformity depend on nitriding process parameters.
Failure to obtain a statistically significant reduction in Cr-Zr interdiffusion depth or improved post-exposure stability relative to an untreated control would falsify the hypothesis.

contradictions.description: The treatment is described as converting the outer part of the Cr coating or forming CrN on the coating, whereas the proposed mediator must be at or near the buried Cr/Zr interface. An outer-surface CrN layer and an interfacial diffusion barrier are different locations, and the stated nitriding procedure does not explain how a continuous buried interfacial layer would be produced.
